name: Minimum wage: the teenager whose job is priced out
scope: The Bastiat broken-window move applied to wage floors. T1: a US Senator proposes raising the federal minimum wage to $15/hour to help low-wage workers. The SEEN effect the sponsors advertise is that every currently-employed worker earning $12/hr now earns $15/hr. T2: the UNSEEN worker Milton Friedman kept pointing at -- a 16-year-old with no experience whose value to a small-restaurant employer is around $8/hour. A $15 floor does not raise his wage to $15; it eliminates his JOB entirely because no employer legally can hire him at $15 for $8 worth of work. Friedman's line (1966 Newsweek column, Free to Choose 1980): 'The minimum wage law is most properly described as a law saying employers must discriminate against people who have low skills.' T3: the substitute-toward-capital margin -- after Seattle's phased wage floor reached $15 in 2017-18, McDonald's, Panera, and Wendy's rolled out self-order KIOSKS at scale; touch-screens do not need a wage. The kiosk is the mechanized answer to the wage floor; the entry-level cashier's job is the UNSEEN cost, replaced by capital equipment that only became worth buying once labor was made more expensive by law. T4: the Card and Krueger 1994 New Jersey vs Pennsylvania fast-food study (American Economic Review) reported little short-run job loss and became the mainstream citation; Neumark and Wascher's follow-up work (Minimum Wages, MIT Press 2008; 2000 AER reply) documents that the Card-Krueger finding disappears in long-run panels, in payroll data (rather than phone-survey employment counts), and in analyses that let employers substitute hours, benefits, and automation. T5: Thomas Sowell's summary in Basic Economics -- there is no such thing as an employer who 'refuses to pay a decent wage'; there are only employers who value particular workers below the floor and hire NO ONE at that skill level. Sowell's chapter title on the topic: 'The chronically-unemployed teenager IS the price of the minimum wage.' Historical anchor: US teenage unemployment rate averaged ~10% in the 1950s at a low real minimum wage; it has averaged ~15-20% since the wage floor was raised repeatedly in the 1970s onward, with catastrophic rates in black-teen cohorts (per Walter Williams, Race and Economics 2011 -- CORROBORATE AT BUILD exact figures).
source: PRIMARY: Milton Friedman, Free to Choose (1980) ch 8; Sowell, Basic Economics (5th ed 2015) ch 10; Neumark and Wascher, Minimum Wages (MIT Press 2008); Card and Krueger, 'Minimum Wages and Employment' AER 84 no 4 (Sept 1994). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Minimum wage in the United States', 'Card-Krueger', 'Neumark-Wascher' (browser, 2026-09-05) -- the 1994 NJ-PA study, the phone-survey vs payroll-data critique, Seattle's 2017-18 phased $15 floor and the Seattle Minimum Wage Study team (UW / Vigdor et al 2017 NBER working paper 23532 finding hours cut ~9% for low-wage workers), the McDonald's kiosk rollout timing. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact Seattle Minimum Wage Study hours-loss figure (9.4% cited widely), exact Walter Williams teenage-unemployment historical series, exact Friedman Newsweek column date.
framing_note: Flagship applied-Bastiat ladder. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (a specific 16-year-old whose $8/hr value cannot legally meet a $15 floor -- the job simply DOES NOT EXIST at that price) and T3 (the McDonald's kiosk as the visible physical answer to Seattle's wage floor). SCENE-LED: T1 opens on a specific Senate proposal, not 'the minimum wage causes...' RECOGNITION-NOT-VERDICT (LOAD-BEARING): stem gives the advocate's proposal; answer names Friedman's or Sowell's REASONING MOVE (the worker priced out is unseen; the kiosk is the substitution margin; judge by results not intentions), NEVER 'the minimum wage is bad'. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: if the stem describes the kiosk substitution, the answer is not 'workers lose jobs' (restatement) -- it is the NAMED move (capital-for-labor substitution at the margin), the NAMED critic (Friedman, Sowell, Neumark), or the NAMED study (Card-Krueger 1994, Neumark-Wascher 2000). DISTRACTOR MINE: other reasoning moves applied to other policies (rent-control's unseen unbuilt housing, tariff's unseen consumer, moral hazard from bailouts), other minimum-wage-adjacent policies (living-wage ordinances, tipped-worker carve-outs), other 20th-century labor economists. BASTIAT PATTERN check: answer hierarchy hits seen-vs-unseen (T2, T3), knowledge-problem (employer knowing individual worker productivity better than a legislator, T4), and 'compared to what' (T5 Sowell). CHOICE PARITY: if the answer is a NAMED CRITIC, all four choices are named 20th-century economists; if it is a NAMED MOVE, all four are named reasoning moves used honestly elsewhere.
history_overlap: None significant -- economics-reasoning lane owns the wage-floor debate. HISTORY owns the political passage of specific bills; here the bills are the setup, not the subject.

name: Rent control: the apartment building that never gets built
scope: Applied seen/unseen for the classic price-ceiling case. T1: a City Council proposes freezing rents on existing units to keep housing 'affordable'. SEEN effect: current tenants pay less month-to-month than they otherwise would. T2: the UNSEEN housing STOCK Assar Lindbeck (Swedish economist, no libertarian) famously called out -- 'In many cases rent control appears to be the most efficient technique presently known to destroy a city -- except for bombing.' The apartment buildings a developer would have built but does not, because the future rents are capped below construction cost, do not exist to be counted. T3: NYC's rent-stabilization system, dating in its current form to the Emergency Tenant Protection Act 1974 and layered on top of the WWII-era rent controls, now covers roughly 966,000 apartments (NYC HPD 2023 Housing Vacancy Survey -- CORROBORATE AT BUILD). NYC construction of new rental housing per capita has run below the US average for decades; the covered units are chronically undermaintained because landlord return-on-repair is capped. T4: Stockholm's rent-control system produces a city-run WAITING LIST -- the average wait for a first-hand rental contract in central Stockholm reached ~20 years by the mid-2010s (Stockholm Bostadsformedlingen figures, widely reported by SVT and The Economist 2015). The UNSEEN family that never gets an apartment does not appear in the seen-tenant count. T5: the black market Bastiat's method predicts and rent-controlled cities always produce -- 'KEY MONEY' side payments (a one-time up-front bribe to get a covered lease), off-books sublets, phantom renovations to reclassify units. Rent Control: Myths and Realities (Fraser Institute, ed. Block and Olsen, 1981) collects the international evidence; Diamond, McQuade, and Qian's 2019 AER paper 'The Effects of Rent Control Expansion on Tenants, Landlords, and Inequality' finds that San Francisco's 1994 rent-control expansion caused affected landlords to reduce their rental housing supply by 15%, worsening the long-run housing shortage the policy claimed to fix.
source: PRIMARY: Diamond, McQuade, Qian, 'The Effects of Rent Control Expansion' AER 109 no 9 (Sept 2019); Block and Olsen eds, Rent Control: Myths and Realities (Fraser Institute 1981) -- the Lindbeck quote is from Lindbeck's essay in that volume, originally The Political Economy of the New Left (Harper 1971). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Rent regulation', 'Rent regulation in New York', 'Rent control in Sweden', 'Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act', 'Stockholm housing queue' (browser, 2026-09-05) -- NYC's Emergency Tenant Protection Act 1974, Stockholm's ~20-year queue, Diamond-McQuade-Qian's 15% supply-reduction figure. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact NYC 2023 HVS stabilized-unit count (~966K is the widely-cited figure), exact Lindbeck quote wording.
framing_note: The classic price-ceiling applied-Bastiat ladder. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (a Swedish socialist economist saying rent control destroys cities more efficiently than bombing) and T4 (a real capital city with a 20-year waitlist to rent an apartment). SCENE-LED: T1 opens on a City Council session, not 'rent control is...' RECOGNITION-NOT-VERDICT: the answer names the reasoning MOVE (unseen unbuilt housing, unseen queue, black-market side payments) or the named critic (Lindbeck, Diamond-McQuade-Qian, Sowell), never 'rent control is bad'. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: if the stem describes the 20-year queue, the answer is not 'people wait a long time' -- it is the NAMED CITY (Stockholm), the NAMED MECHANISM (housing supply not built because future rents are capped below cost), or the NAMED FALLBACK (the informal side-payment market, 'key money'). DISTRACTOR MINE: other price ceilings (gasoline price caps 1970s producing gas lines, Diocletian's Edict on Maximum Prices 301 AD, Venezuela's price controls under Maduro), other named housing policies (mortgage interest deduction, LIHTC low-income tax credits, Section 8 vouchers), other named cities with rent regimes (Berlin's 2020 Mietendeckel struck down by the constitutional court 2021, Los Angeles, San Francisco). CHOICE PARITY: if the answer is a NAMED CITY, all four choices are cities with named housing regimes; if it is a REASONING MOVE, all four are reasoning moves used honestly elsewhere.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns Stockholm and NYC as places; here they are policy laboratories. HISTORY owns the WWII rent-control origins as political fact; here the policy sequence is the subject.

name: Tariffs: the consumer who pays and does not know it
scope: Bastiat's petition-of-candlemakers move applied to modern trade policy. T1: in March 2018 the Trump administration announces 25% tariffs on imported steel and 10% on imported aluminum, on the stated rationale of protecting US steel jobs. SEEN: US Steel and Nucor reopen or expand a handful of facilities; specific mill workers in Granite City IL, Ashland KY are cited by the administration. T2: the UNSEEN consumer Bastiat named in 1845 -- the American car buyer, appliance buyer, canned-food buyer, and construction customer whose prices rise because steel input costs rise. The Peterson Institute for International Economics (Bown and Zhang, PIIE Working Paper 20-14, 2020) calculated the 2018-19 steel and aluminum tariffs cost US consumers approximately $900,000 PER STEEL JOB SAVED per year -- because the raised prices are spread across every buyer of steel-intensive goods (CORROBORATE AT BUILD -- Cato and PIIE both cite this per-job cost). T3: the DOWNSTREAM job losses in steel-USING industries. The Federal Reserve Board study by Flaaen and Pierce (FEDS 2019-086, December 2019) found the 2018 tariffs caused a NET LOSS of about 75,000 US manufacturing jobs in steel-consuming sectors -- larger than the ~1,000 jobs added in primary steel. Every downstream industry (auto parts, machinery, canned food) faced higher input costs and shed workers. T4: the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of June 1930 as the historical anchor -- Herbert Hoover signed it against a petition from 1,028 economists led by Paul Douglas, raising average tariffs on dutiable imports to roughly 45%. Foreign retaliation followed within months; US exports collapsed from $5.2B (1929) to $1.7B (1933); Smoot-Hawley did not CAUSE the Great Depression (that was monetary, per Friedman-Schwartz) but it turned a recession into a global trade collapse. T5: Bastiat's petition-of-candlemakers reductio -- if raising the price of a domestic good by taxing its cheaper foreign substitute makes a nation richer, why not tax the SUN to protect candlemakers? The 1930 economists' petition Hoover ignored used exactly this argument; the 2018 tariffs vindicated it once more. Douglas Irwin's Peddling Protectionism (2011) is the standard history of Smoot-Hawley; his Free Trade Under Fire (4th ed 2015) applies the same reasoning to modern trade policy.
source: PRIMARY: Bown and Zhang, 'Measuring Trump's 2018 Trade Protection' PIIE Working Paper 20-14 (Feb 2020); Flaaen and Pierce, 'Disentangling the Effects of the 2018-2019 Tariffs' FEDS Working Paper 2019-086 (Dec 2019); Irwin, Peddling Protectionism: Smoot-Hawley and the Great Depression (Princeton 2011). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Trump tariffs', 'Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act', 'Petition of 1,028 economists' (browser, 2026-09-05) -- the March 2018 Section 232 tariffs, the ~$900K per-job-saved figure widely quoted from Cato and PIIE, the Fed's Flaaen-Pierce 75,000-job downstream loss, Smoot-Hawley signed June 17 1930, US exports collapsed 1929-33. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact 1,028 signatory count on the 1930 petition (some sources 1,028 some 1,032), exact per-job cost figure, exact 1929 vs 1933 export dollars.
framing_note: The applied-Bastiat trade-policy ladder. Dinner-test payoff: T2 ($900,000 spent by US consumers PER steel job protected -- absurd on its face) and T3 (a Fed study finding the tariffs cost more downstream jobs than they saved upstream). SCENE-LED: T1 opens on the March 2018 announcement, not 'tariffs are...' RECOGNITION-NOT-VERDICT: the answer names the reasoning MOVE (unseen consumer, unseen downstream employer, reductio via candlemakers) or the NAMED critic (Bastiat, Irwin, PIIE, the 1930 signatories), never 'tariffs are bad' or 'free trade is good'. Both administrations' positions are set up honestly. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: if the stem gives the $900K per-job figure, the answer is not 'tariffs are inefficient' -- it is the SPECIFIC UNSEEN group (auto-parts buyers, canned-food buyers), the NAMED STUDY (PIIE 2020), or the NAMED MOVE (concentrated benefit + dispersed cost). DISTRACTOR MINE: other trade policies (NAFTA 1994, WTO accession of China 2001, USMCA 2020), other Bastiat sophisms (negative railway, candlemakers), other reasoning moves (Olson concentrated-benefit + dispersed-cost, moral hazard). CHOICE PARITY: if the answer is a NAMED YEAR, all four are trade-policy years; if a NAMED ECONOMIST, all four are trade-policy economists.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns Smoot-Hawley as a political-legislative event (Hoover's decision, Senate votes); economics owns the trade-collapse reasoning. Do NOT seed a rung on Hoover's biography.

name: Cash for Clunkers 2009: 690,000 used cars destroyed
scope: Bastiat's broken-window applied to a specific $3B federal program. T1: the Car Allowance Rebate System (CARS Act), signed by President Obama June 24 2009 and running July-August 2009, offered car buyers a $3,500-$4,500 rebate for trading in a working older vehicle -- provided the trade-in was DESTROYED (engine seized by pouring sodium silicate into the oil, then crushed). SEEN: 677,842 new vehicles sold under the program (final DOT figure, EPA 2013 assessment), a visible short-term auto-industry boost, GM and Chrysler sales climbing during the program window. T2: the UNSEEN Bastiat named -- the DESTROYED used cars, roughly 690,000 vehicles under a mandate that all trade-ins be scrapped so the rebate money did not just subsidize what would have happened anyway. Each of those cars would have gone on to serve a second-hand buyer, a mechanic's parts inventory, or a charity donation. T3: the second UNSEEN -- the poor households who buy used cars. Cash for Clunkers destroyed roughly 690,000 running vehicles in the $1,500-$4,500 blue-book range, which is exactly the range low-income and student buyers actually purchase. Used-car prices rose ~10% in the year after the program (Manheim Used Vehicle Value Index, 2009-10 -- CORROBORATE AT BUILD exact figure), pricing out the households the auto stimulus was said to help. T4: Ted Gayer and Emily Parker at Brookings ('Cash for Clunkers: An Evaluation of the Car Allowance Rebate System', Brookings, October 2013) found the program pulled sales forward by about 380,000 vehicles (most of the 'new' sales would have happened within 6-9 months anyway), created net zero long-run jobs, and produced CO2 savings at a cost of roughly $91-$301 per ton -- well above the EPA's own social cost of carbon. T5: Bastiat's move made concrete -- the SEEN sale is the shiny new car in the buyer's driveway; the UNSEEN is the used car that would have transported a Georgia family to work, the mechanic's income from servicing it, the tools the buyer did not buy because he chose a new car, and the resources embodied in the trade-in that were poured into an oil pan instead of driven. Hazlitt's Economics in One Lesson (1946) is a book-length restatement of this exact move; Cash for Clunkers is the 21st-century worked example.
source: PRIMARY: Gayer and Parker, 'Cash for Clunkers: An Evaluation of the Car Allowance Rebate System' (Brookings Economic Studies, Oct 2013); DOT CARS program final report (NHTSA, 2009); Mian and Sufi, 'The Effects of Fiscal Stimulus: Evidence from the 2009 Cash for Clunkers Program' QJE 127 no 3 (Aug 2012) -- finds essentially all sales pulled forward, reversed within 7-9 months. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Car Allowance Rebate System', 'Cash for Clunkers' (browser, 2026-09-05) -- signed June 24 2009 by Obama, ran July-August 2009, 690,114 vehicles destroyed final total, engine-seizure sodium-silicate procedure required, Brookings and QJE evaluations. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact Brookings per-ton CO2 cost range, exact Manheim used-vehicle price movement in 2009-10.
framing_note: Applied-broken-window ladder with a physical, concrete answer set (real cars, sodium silicate, poor families needing transport). Dinner-test payoff: T1 (a federal program that required destroying working cars by seizing their engines with liquid glass) and T3 (used-car prices rose 10% the year after, pricing out poor households the program claimed to help). SCENE-LED: T1 opens on the signed CARS Act, not 'the program aimed to...' RECOGNITION-NOT-VERDICT: the answer names Bastiat's move (destroyed working stock is unseen alternate use; poor used-car buyers are the unseen victims; sales are pulled forward not created) or the NAMED evaluators (Gayer-Parker Brookings, Mian-Sufi QJE 2012), never 'the stimulus was bad'. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: if the stem describes the engine-destruction procedure, the answer is not 'cars were destroyed' -- it is the specific UNSEEN buyer (the used-car market), the NAMED evaluator, or the NAMED MOVE (pulled-forward sales, alternate-use of resources). DISTRACTOR MINE: other 2009 stimulus programs (ARRA infrastructure, first-time homebuyer credit, unemployment insurance extensions), other 'destroy to create' cases (WWII bond drives, agricultural set-asides), other reasoning moves. name: Fiscal stimulus and the multiplier: the private investment crowded out
scope: Bastiat's method applied to Keynesian aggregate-demand policy. T1: in January 2009 the incoming Obama administration's Council of Economic Advisers (Christina Romer, Jared Bernstein) publishes 'The Job Impact of the American Recovery and Reinvestment Plan' estimating a government-spending multiplier of about 1.55 -- $1 of federal spending would raise GDP by $1.55 -- and predicts unemployment would peak below 8% if the $787B ARRA passed. Unemployment reached 10.0% in October 2009 with ARRA fully in effect. T2: the UNSEEN Bastiat's method predicts -- for every dollar the government spends, that dollar came from somewhere: taxed away from a household who no longer buys what they would have bought, borrowed from a lender who no longer funds a private investment, or printed such that Cantillon-effect winners capture it before prices adjust. The SEEN is the road crew and the ribbon-cutting; the UNSEEN is the private capital that dollar would have financed. T3: Robert Barro's counter-multiplier estimates (Macroeconomics: A Modern Approach and 'Government Spending, Taxation, and the Multiplier' Mercatus 2011) -- using WWII spending as the biggest natural-experiment shock, Barro estimates the peacetime government spending multiplier is closer to 0.4-0.7. Below 1 means: for every additional dollar of government spending, private spending falls MORE than the direct government injection, and total output rises by less than the dollar spent (net loss). T4: Valerie Ramey's careful VAR estimates (Ramey, 'Can Government Purchases Stimulate the Economy?' JEL 2011) find defense-spending multipliers of 0.6-1.1 depending on specification; peacetime civilian multipliers cluster below 1. Cogan-Cwik-Taylor-Wieland's 2010 J. Econ. Dynamics paper found the Romer-Bernstein 1.55 assumed away crowding-out; recalculated with standard New Keynesian frictions the multiplier is 0.6-0.7. T5: Bastiat's cutting move -- to the Keynesian claim 'spending creates income', Bastiat's method asks: WHOSE spending? The government's dollar had to come from a taxpayer's pocket or a lender's savings; the road crew's income was the taxpayer's foregone consumption; that consumption was ALSO income for whoever the taxpayer would have hired. The multiplier debate is about whether the reshuffled dollar produces MORE aggregate income than the private dollar would have; the historical evidence (ARRA 2009, Japan's lost decade 1990s stimulus packages, EU stimulus post-2008) is uniformly disappointing. Hazlitt's Economics in One Lesson chapter 'Public Works Mean Taxes' is the 1946 statement of the move; Hayek's 1932 letter to The Times (against Keynes's public-works proposals) is the older statement.
source: PRIMARY: Romer and Bernstein, 'The Job Impact of the American Recovery and Reinvestment Plan' (CEA, January 2009); Barro, 'Government Spending, Taxation, and the Multiplier' (Mercatus Working Paper, 2011); Ramey, 'Can Government Purchases Stimulate the Economy?' Journal of Economic Literature 49 no 3 (Sept 2011); Cogan, Cwik, Taylor, Wieland, 'New Keynesian versus Old Keynesian Government Spending Multipliers' Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control 34 no 3 (2010). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'American Recovery and Reinvestment Act', 'Fiscal multiplier', 'Robert Barro' (browser, 2026-09-05) -- Romer-Bernstein 1.55 multiplier, sub-8% peak prediction, actual 10% peak, Barro's WWII multiplier estimates, Ramey's VAR range. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact Cogan-Cwik-Taylor-Wieland recalculated multiplier, exact October 2009 peak unemployment figure (10.0% is the BLS series).
framing_note: The macro-multiplier ladder is the hardest reasoning move in the pillar; keep it grade-10 by anchoring on the ARRA specific prediction and the historical outcome. Dinner-test payoff: T1 (a government predicted unemployment stays below 8% if the stimulus passes; the stimulus passed and unemployment hit 10%) and T5 (a road crew's paycheck was ALSO income for someone else before the government took it -- the multiplier argument depends on which use produces more downstream). SCENE-LED: T1 opens on the CEA memo, not 'the multiplier debate concerns...' RECOGNITION-NOT-VERDICT: the answer names the reasoning MOVE (crowding-out, opportunity cost of taxed/borrowed dollars, the multiplier's sub-1 estimates) or the NAMED critic (Barro, Ramey, Hayek 1932), never 'Keynesian stimulus doesn't work'. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: if the stem describes the Romer-Bernstein 1.55 estimate, the answer is not 'stimulus was too small' (a Keynesian move) or 'stimulus doesn't work' (a verdict) -- it is the NAMED counter-estimate (Barro's 0.4-0.7), the NAMED MOVE (crowding out of private investment), or Bastiat's identification (dollar had to come from a taxpayer/lender/printer). DISTRACTOR MINE: other applied-Bastiat cases (broken window, Cash for Clunkers, tariffs), other macroeconomics moves (Ricardian equivalence, rational expectations), other named economists. BASTIAT PATTERN check: at T5 the answer is the specific alternative use of the resources, NOT 'stimulus is bad'. CHOICE PARITY: if the answer is a NAMED ECONOMIST, all four are macro economists; if a NUMERIC MULTIPLIER, all four are plausible multiplier estimates from the literature.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns ARRA's political passage; economics owns the multiplier evaluation. Japan's lost decade appears as a stimulus case, not a political history.

name: The US Sugar Program: candy jobs that fled to Mexico
scope: A concrete, easy-to-visualize applied-Bastiat case with a physical answer set. T1: the US Sugar Program (Sugar Act 1934, currently structured under the 2018 Farm Bill) uses import quotas (TRQs), price-support loans, and marketing allotments to hold the US wholesale sugar price at roughly TWICE the world price -- typical US price ~35 cents/lb vs world ~17 cents/lb in the 2010s (US GAO 2000 and 2013 reports; CBO 2017 -- CORROBORATE AT BUILD exact spread). T2: the SEEN side -- roughly 4,000 US sugar-beet and sugar-cane growers benefit substantially; the Fanjul family in Florida (owners of Domino Sugar and Florida Crystals) is the paradigm case of a small, politically-organized group of beneficiaries. T3: the UNSEEN downstream -- Bastiat's method predicts that any US industry that USES sugar as an input faces double the world's input cost, and will move production to where sugar is cheap. LifeSavers moved its Holland MI plant to Montreal in 2003 because Canadian sugar costs half as much. Kraft Foods closed its Life Savers plant in 2003 citing sugar costs. Ferrara Pan Candy moved much of its Chicago production to Mexico in the 2000s. Brach's moved to Mexico 2003. Total downstream US candy job losses have been estimated at ~10,000+ (Commerce Department 2006 report -- CORROBORATE AT BUILD). T4: the concentrated-benefit / dispersed-cost logic (Olson) -- ~4,000 sugar-growing operations get millions each in supported prices and quota rents; ~330M US consumers pay a few dollars extra per year for candy, soda, and baked goods, and never know the program exists. The Sugar Program has survived every Farm Bill for 90 years because the beneficiary group is small and organized and the cost group is enormous and unaware. T5: Bastiat's petition-of-candlemakers reductio replayed in reverse -- the Sugar Program is a real 21st-century law protecting a domestic industry from cheaper foreign competition. The pupil should hear the argument the sugar growers make (national security, rural jobs, protecting an American industry) and be able to identify it as exactly the argument the imaginary candlemakers made against the sun in 1845. Cato's 'Rethinking the US Sugar Program' (Chris Edwards + Ike Brannon, Cato Policy Analysis 2018) is the standard modern critique.
source: PRIMARY: US Government Accountability Office, 'Sugar Program: Supporting Sugar Prices Has Increased Users' Costs While Benefiting Producers' GAO/RCED-00-126 (2000); GAO update 2013; US Department of Commerce, 'Employment Changes in US Food Manufacturing: The Impact of Sugar Prices' (Feb 2006); Cato Institute policy analyses (Edwards, Brannon). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'US Sugar Program', 'Fanjul brothers', 'Sugar tariff' (browser, 2026-09-05) -- price-double-world figure, candy-industry relocations (LifeSavers 2003 to Montreal, Ferrara Pan to Mexico), Fanjul family concentration, Farm Bill perpetuation. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact US-vs-world price spread by year, exact LifeSavers move date, exact Commerce Department job-loss figure.
framing_note: A concrete, viscerally clear applied-Bastiat case with a memorable answer set (LifeSavers moved to Canada). Dinner-test payoff: T3 (a US candy plant moved to Canada because Canadian sugar was half the price -- the American law INCREASED foreign employment) and T4 (a 90-year-old program that survives every Farm Bill because 4,000 growers organize and 330M consumers don't). SCENE-LED: T1 opens on the actual price spread, not 'the sugar program is...' RECOGNITION-NOT-VERDICT: the answer names Bastiat's UNSEEN downstream employer, Olson's concentrated benefit + dispersed cost, or the NAMED move (candlemakers reductio applied to real 21st-century law) -- never 'the sugar program is bad'. DISTRACTOR MINE: other tariff-affected industries (steel, textiles, ethanol), other named agribusiness dynasties, other Bastiat sophisms. name: Occupational licensing: 1,600 hours to braid hair
scope: The concentrated-benefit / dispersed-cost move applied to entry barriers. T1: as of the 2010s roughly one in four US workers requires a government license to legally work in their occupation (Kleiner and Krueger 2013, Journal of Labor Economics -- CORROBORATE AT BUILD exact share; often cited as 25-29%); up from ~5% in the 1950s (Kleiner, Licensing Occupations 2006). Licenses now cover hair braiders, interior designers, florists, tour guides, casket sellers, and eyebrow threaders in various states. T2: the SEEN advocates say licensing protects consumers from unsafe practitioners. T3: the UNSEEN -- the entrepreneur BLOCKED from entering the trade. Iowa requires 2,100 hours of cosmetology school to legally braid hair professionally (Institute for Justice, 'License to Work' 2022 -- CORROBORATE AT BUILD exact hour count); the school costs ~$20,000 and teaches almost nothing relevant to African-style hair braiding. Melony Armstrong (Tupelo MS), Isis Brantley (Dallas TX), and the JJR Cornrows Inc. plaintiffs sued their state cosmetology boards through IJ; Louisiana's florist license (yes -- a state test to sell flowers) was defended in court by incumbent florists (Meadows v. Odom 2005). T4: the concentrated-benefit / dispersed-cost logic (Olson) -- the SMALL group of INCUMBENT practitioners lobbies intensely to keep the license (fewer competitors = higher prices for their services); the LARGE group of would-be entrants and consumers pays higher prices and never organizes. The typical state cosmetology board is composed of licensed cosmetologists; they set the entry rules for their own competitors. This is Stigler's 1971 regulatory-capture pattern -- the regulator serves the regulated. T5: Milton Friedman's Capitalism and Freedom (1962) chapter on 'Occupational Licensure' -- Friedman argued that licensure of physicians (the AMA's core function since 1847) restricts supply and raises prices; the same argument scales down to hair braiders and florists. Friedman's cutting reformulation: 'What licensure protects the consumer FROM is not incompetent practitioners; it is competition.' The Institute for Justice's Chip Mellor and Clint Bolick have built a 30-year litigation record dismantling the most absurd examples one Sixth Circuit or Fifth Circuit case at a time.

name: Import quotas: the 1980s Japanese auto VER
scope: The applied-Bastiat case where the mechanism was a QUOTA (not a tariff) and it made the point sharper. T1: in May 1981 the Reagan administration negotiated a 'voluntary export restraint' (VER) with Japan capping Japanese passenger-car exports to the US at 1.68 million vehicles per year; the cap was renegotiated upward through the 1980s and formally ended in 1994. Its stated rationale was to protect Detroit (GM, Ford, Chrysler) from Japanese competition. T2: the SEEN side -- Detroit got breathing space, and specifically UAW jobs in Michigan, Ohio, and Indiana were the visible beneficiaries. T3: the UNSEEN American car buyer -- Robert Crandall of Brookings estimated the VER raised US car prices approximately $1,000 per vehicle (1983 dollars) for BOTH Japanese and American cars (because domestic makers raised prices under the reduced competition umbrella). Later work by Feenstra ('Voluntary Export Restraints in US Autos, 1980-1981', in Baldwin ed, 1988, NBER volume) put the total consumer cost at ~$5-8 billion/year. T4: the second UNSEEN -- LOW-INCOME buyers were hurt worst. Because the quota was on VEHICLES not on value, Japanese makers responded rationally by shifting production to HIGHER-END models (each unit had to earn more profit under the cap). The Honda Accord, Toyota Camry, and Nissan Maxima grew larger, better-equipped, more expensive; the cheap Civic-class hatchback disappeared upward. The consumer priced out of a $4,500 Japanese econobox was the UNSEEN victim; the visible Michigan autoworker was the SEEN beneficiary. T5: the third UNSEEN -- the QUOTA RENT went to Japan, not to the US Treasury. Because the cap gave each Japanese exporter a scarcity value, the price markup accrued as PROFIT to Toyota and Honda (estimated ~$2,000 per car of quota rent). A TARIFF at the same restrictiveness would have collected that revenue for the Treasury; the VER left it with the foreign producer. Feenstra's calculation: the VER was the WORST possible way to give the same protection -- higher consumer cost, no revenue, and windfall to the very foreign producers the policy claimed to punish. Bastiat's method surfaces all three unseens; a legislator seeing only Detroit jobs sees only the seen.

name: The broken window applied to war and disaster 'stimulus'
scope: Bastiat's method turned against the 'destruction creates prosperity' claim. T1: at the end of World War II, the US had roughly 12 million men under arms; by June 1946 more than 8 million had been demobilized. Keynesian economists including Alvin Hansen predicted a return to depression -- the argument being that wartime spending had 'lifted' the economy out of the 1930s and its removal would collapse it. T2: what actually happened -- despite federal spending falling from $84B (1945) to $30B (1946) to $34B (1947), and 8M soldiers returning to the labor force, unemployment stayed around 4% in 1946-47 and real private-sector output surged. Henry Hazlitt in Economics in One Lesson (1946) called this the definitive real-world refutation of the broken-window argument for war: private demand and investment absorbed the released resources within months. T3: Bastiat's method applied to Hurricane Katrina 2005 -- major news outlets and some economists (including Paul Krugman in various columns) argued the ~$100B in rebuilding would 'stimulate' the Gulf economy. Bastiat's UNSEEN: the destroyed homes and businesses had to be REBUILT, meaning the resources that rebuilt them could NOT be used elsewhere. Louisianans and Mississippians ended 2006 with the SAME houses they had in mid-2005 -- minus a year's worth of alternative economic activity, minus deaths and injuries. T4: applied to war -- when Krugman wrote (September 14, 2001, NYT column, later much-quoted) that the 9/11 attacks would 'do some economic good' via rebuilding demand, Bastiat's method surfaces the unseen: the office buildings had to be rebuilt at the cost of not building other new office buildings; the labor absorbed by the World Trade Center reconstruction could not build homes in Queens. Krugman later walked back the framing; the broken-window objection to it remains standard classroom material at Cato, Mercatus, and every Austrian-friendly economics program. T5: the deep move -- the seen benefit of any reconstruction is the SAME as any private construction spending; the unseen cost is what was DESTROYED. Bastiat's shopkeeper who breaks his own window is one window POORER, not one window's-worth of glazier-employment richer. The 1946 postwar experience is the largest peacetime natural experiment in demobilization the US ever ran; the Keynesian prediction of depression was empirically wrong; the Austrian-Bastiat prediction (private demand absorbs the released resources) was empirically right.

name: Social Security: the retirement check and the unseen alternative
scope: Bastiat's method applied to the largest US transfer program. T1: the US Social Security program (Social Security Act 1935 under FDR) collects a 12.4% payroll tax (6.2% employer + 6.2% employee, with employees seeing only their own half) on wages up to a capped base (~$168,600 in 2024) and pays monthly benefits to retirees, disabled workers, and survivors. Total benefits in 2023: ~$1.4 trillion; total beneficiaries: ~67 million. T2: the SEEN -- retirees receive a monthly check. For many low-income retirees, Social Security is the majority of retirement income; the program is politically untouchable ('third rail of American politics'). T3: the UNSEEN Bastiat's method surfaces -- (1) the payroll tax REDUCES wage income the earner would have SPENT OR SAVED, so private savings and consumption are lower than they would have been; (2) if the 12.4% had been invested in a private retirement account with historical stock-market returns (~7% real annualized long-run), the average earner would retire with a substantially larger nest egg than Social Security provides; Milton Friedman calculated (Free to Choose 1980) that the median worker's expected Social Security payout has an INTERNAL RATE OF RETURN of roughly 1-2%, compared to the historical 6-7% real return on diversified stocks. T4: the demographic UNSEEN -- Social Security is 'pay-as-you-go' (current workers' taxes fund current retirees). In 1950 the worker-to-beneficiary ratio was ~16.5:1; today it is ~2.7:1; the OASDI Trust Fund's own trustees project reserve depletion around 2033-35, after which benefits would automatically be cut ~20% unless Congress acts (SSA Trustees Report 2024 -- CORROBORATE AT BUILD exact year). T5: Bastiat's method -- the visible retiree check is real; the UNSEEN alternative is what the payroll-tax dollars would have compounded to in a private account over 45 years. Friedman's move is not 'Social Security is bad' but 'the counterfactual comparison is the private savings foregone.' Personal-retirement-account reform (Chile 1981 under Jose Pinera; George W. Bush's 2005 attempt in the US, defeated) is the applied policy question the reasoning frames.

name: Solyndra 2011: the green loan guarantee that failed
scope: The concentrated-benefit / knowledge-problem case for green industrial policy. T1: Solyndra was a California solar-panel manufacturer that received a $535 million loan guarantee from the US Department of Energy under Section 1705 of the Energy Policy Act 2005, expedited under the 2009 ARRA stimulus. President Obama visited the plant in May 2010 calling it 'the true engine of economic growth'; Solyndra filed for bankruptcy September 2011, laid off 1,100 workers, and defaulted on the loan. T2: the SEEN case for the guarantee -- clean-energy jobs, technology-race-with-China framing, cylindrical-solar-panel technology that would supposedly outcompete Chinese flat panels. T3: the UNSEEN Bastiat's method surfaces -- (1) private investors had passed on the deeper rounds of Solyndra funding because cylindrical panels required much more copper-indium-gallium-selenide material per watt than flat panels, and world silicon prices were collapsing (from ~$400/kg in 2008 to ~$40/kg by 2011); (2) the $535M could not simultaneously be doing anything else -- other startups did not get it; (3) the government's loan-guarantee decisions rewarded political connectivity (major Solyndra investor Argonaut Ventures / George Kaiser had been an Obama fundraiser) rather than technical merit. T4: Hayek's knowledge problem in Bastiat clothes -- a private venture capitalist who puts his OWN money at risk has strong incentives to research the silicon-price trajectory, the manufacturing cost curves, and the competing technologies. A DOE loan officer using taxpayer money faces no such personal cost of being wrong. When private VCs pass and public loan officers approve, Hayek's move surfaces: the dispersed knowledge of thousands of private investors was signaling 'this technology will not compete' and the public agency ignored the signal. T5: the deeper Bastiat move -- the SEEN failure of $535M is dramatic and photogenic; the UNSEEN failure is the ~$16.4 billion the DOE Section 1705 program lent to 30+ recipients (of which Solyndra was one; Abound Solar, Fisker Automotive, and A123 Systems also went bankrupt), all evaluated by the same politically-influenced process. Wonderful successes may exist in that portfolio; the question is whether the $16.4B produced more than the same money left in private hands would have. Bastiat's method says: compare the seen benefit to the unseen alternative use of the same capital.

name: TARP and bailouts: moral hazard and the 2023 SVB sequel
scope: The moral-hazard reasoning move applied across two bailout episodes. T1: the Troubled Asset Relief Program (TARP), signed October 3, 2008 by President Bush, authorized $700 billion for the Treasury to purchase troubled assets and, ultimately, to buy preferred stock in major banks (Bank of America, Citigroup, JPMorgan, Wells Fargo, Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley et al). T2: the SEEN justification -- prevent a cascading financial-system collapse that would have crushed Main Street depositors; most TARP funds were eventually repaid; the program 'made money' on paper. T3: the UNSEEN Bastiat's method surfaces -- the PRECEDENT. A bank creditor who lends to a systemically-important bank now knows that in a crisis, the federal government will make him whole. This CHANGES BEHAVIOR going forward: creditors demand LESS risk premium from big banks, banks take on MORE risk knowing they will be rescued, and the system becomes MORE fragile. This is what economists call MORAL HAZARD, and it is a Bastiat-style unseen because the changed-behavior effect does not appear in the year of the bailout; it appears in the next crisis. T4: the March 2023 sequel -- Silicon Valley Bank failed on March 10, 2023 after a classic bank run triggered by unrealized losses on its long-duration Treasury holdings (bought at 2020-21 zero rates, marked down after the Fed's 2022-23 tightening). The FDIC insures deposits up to $250K; SVB had ~93% of deposits UNINSURED. On March 12 the Treasury, Fed, and FDIC jointly announced ALL SVB depositors would be made whole -- including uninsured ones. Signature Bank got the same treatment days later. T5: Bastiat's method identifying what the 2008 precedent produced -- the SVB depositors, largely tech companies and venture capitalists, had CHOSEN to keep more than $250K in a single uninsured account; the market signal was 'diversify your bank exposure or lose it in a run'. The bailout ELIMINATED that market signal. Walter Bagehot's Lombard Street (1873) had the classic central-bank rule for crises: 'lend freely, at high rates, against good collateral' -- meaning the lender-of-last-resort should charge a PUNISHING rate so banks avoid using the facility except in true crisis. The 2023 SVB response gave uninsured depositors a FREE OPTION at zero cost. Anna Schwartz's warning (co-author with Friedman of the 1963 Monetary History): 'The Fed is now in the business of preserving asset values, not merely stabilizing money.'

CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Troubled Asset Relief Program', 'Silicon Valley Bank collapse', 'Moral hazard', 'Walter Bagehot' (browser, 2026-09-05) -- $700B TARP authorization, October 2008 passage, SVB March 10 2023 failure, FDIC/Treasury/Fed joint statement making uninsured depositors whole, Bagehot's rule. name: PPP loans 2020: the concentrated-benefit COVID case
scope: Bastiat and Olson applied to the 2020-21 pandemic small-business support. T1: the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP), part of the CARES Act March 2020, ultimately disbursed ~$800B in forgivable loans to US small businesses on the condition they maintain payroll. The program's stated goal was to prevent mass small-business closures and layoffs during COVID lockdowns. T2: the SEEN side -- millions of small businesses received PPP funds, and the loans were eventually forgiven; small-business closures during 2020-21 were far lower than early projections. T3: the UNSEEN Bastiat's method surfaces -- David Autor, Raj Chetty, and coauthors ('An Evaluation of the Paycheck Protection Program' NBER Working Paper 29669, Jan 2022; JEP 36 no 2 Spring 2022) estimated that PPP preserved 2-3 million job-years at a cost of $170,000-$257,000 PER JOB PRESERVED. The overwhelming majority of PPP funds (66-75%) flowed to firms that would NOT have laid off workers even without PPP, or to owners as increased profit -- Autor et al: '72% of program funds accrued to business owners and shareholders rather than to workers.' T4: the ALLOCATION problem Hayek's knowledge problem predicts -- PPP was distributed through EXISTING BANK RELATIONSHIPS (Bank of America, JPMorgan, etc). Firms with established bank ties got funded in days; firms without them (typically minority-owned and rural firms) waited weeks or missed the first tranche entirely. The intended beneficiaries (fragile small firms) were the least likely to have the bank relationships to access the program quickly. Concentrated benefits went to firms that would have survived anyway; dispersed costs fell on all future taxpayers servicing the $800B in debt. T5: the deeper Bastiat move -- the SEEN preserved jobs are real; the UNSEEN is (a) the ~$600B that flowed to firms that would not have laid off anyone anyway (Chetty et al's inframarginal share) (b) the debt burden on future taxpayers (c) the precedent that any future crisis will trigger a similar broad-based transfer. Cato and Mercatus economists have argued targeted unemployment insurance would have preserved the SAME jobs at a fraction of the cost.

name: Davis-Bacon and prevailing wages: paid to stand idle
scope: The applied-Bastiat case for construction-labor rules on federal projects. T1: the Davis-Bacon Act 1931 (Rep. Robert Bacon R-NY, Sen. James Davis R-PA) requires that federally-funded construction projects pay 'prevailing local wages' -- which the Department of Labor determines through a wage-survey process that, in practice, defaults to the union scale in most metropolitan areas. T2: the SEEN side -- union construction workers on federal projects earn substantially more than non-union workers on comparable private projects; the Act has been the AFL-CIO's core piece of federal-project protection for 90 years. T3: the UNSEEN cost -- federal construction costs are systematically HIGHER than comparable state or private construction. The Beacon Hill Institute and CBO have estimated Davis-Bacon adds 10-15% to federal construction costs; on the $1.2 trillion 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act this is $100-180 billion (CORROBORATE AT BUILD). Every additional dollar of federal cost is a dollar taxed from private users. T4: the historical UNSEEN Davis-Bacon's original supporters admitted -- the 1931 Congressional Record explicitly discusses excluding SOUTHERN BLACK workers who were migrating north to compete for federal-project work at wages below northern union scales. Rep. Bacon in the House debate: 'Colored labor is being brought in to demoralize wage rates.' The Act's original design was overtly to exclude non-union (largely black) labor from federal jobsites; it retains that exclusionary effect even after the racist framing was dropped. T5: Bastiat and Olson combined -- SEEN: union wages on federal projects (concentrated benefit to organized incumbents); UNSEEN: fewer projects at any given federal budget, higher taxes to fund the same infrastructure, lower employment of non-union (often minority or rural) workers who cannot meet the wage-scale threshold. Reformer arguments (Ron Utt at Heritage; Chris Edwards at Cato; the Beacon Hill Institute) have called for repeal every decade since the 1980s; the AFL-CIO's political weight has kept it on the books.

name: School choice: Milton Friedman's 1955 voucher essay
scope: Applied competitive-pressure Bastiat to K-12 education. T1: in 1955 Milton Friedman published 'The Role of Government in Education' (in Robert Solo ed, Economics and the Public Interest, Rutgers UP; reprinted in Capitalism and Freedom 1962 ch 6). Friedman proposed VOUCHERS -- give parents the per-pupil expenditure as a portable credit redeemable at any accredited school. T2: the SEEN status quo -- US public schools are FINANCED AND OPERATED by school districts, funded through property taxes and state formulas. Total US K-12 spending: ~$800 billion/year; per-pupil spending has TRIPLED in real terms since 1970 with no measurable rise in NAEP scores (National Center for Education Statistics -- CORROBORATE AT BUILD figures). T3: the UNSEEN competitive-pressure Bastiat's method surfaces -- because families cannot exit a bad public school without moving house, the school faces almost no competitive pressure to improve. A grocery store where 90% of customers were mandatorily assigned to its checkout would degrade over time; the K-12 system is that grocery store. Chubb and Moe's Politics, Markets, and America's Schools (Brookings 1990) is the classic empirical treatment. T4: the applied-policy cases -- Milwaukee's Parental Choice Program (1990, first US urban voucher), Cleveland's voucher case reaching the Supreme Court (Zelman v. Simmons-Harris 2002 upholding vouchers usable at religious schools), Florida's Tax Credit Scholarship, Arizona's ESA, and the wave of state ESA programs 2023-24 (West Virginia, Iowa, Arkansas, Florida universal, Ohio). name: Zoning: the housing that Glaeser and Gyourko show never gets built
scope: The applied-Bastiat case for local land-use restrictions. T1: US municipalities set land-use rules through ZONING codes -- what types of building are permitted where, minimum lot sizes, height limits, setback requirements, parking mandates, and single-family-only designations. T2: the SEEN side -- residents in restrictive zones enjoy stable neighborhood character, controlled density, and (crucially) higher home values because supply is constrained. T3: the UNSEEN housing Edward Glaeser and Joseph Gyourko's paper 'The Impact of Zoning on Housing Affordability' (NBER 2002, Economic Policy Review 2003) quantified -- they compared the CONSTRUCTION cost of an apartment building to the MARKET price of an apartment in various cities. In Manhattan the difference (which they called the 'zoning tax') was ~$500,000 per apartment in the early 2000s (updated to >$1M by the 2010s -- CORROBORATE AT BUILD). In San Francisco, San Jose, Boston: hundreds of thousands per unit. In Houston, Atlanta, Dallas (looser zoning): essentially zero zoning tax. T4: the concentrated-benefit / dispersed-cost pattern -- SEEN: current homeowners in restrictive zones benefit from higher home values (concentrated benefit to a specific organized group who VOTE IN LOCAL ELECTIONS). name: Certificate of Need: the hospital that never opens
scope: The applied-Bastiat case for healthcare entry-barrier regulation. T1: Certificate of Need (CON) laws are state statutes requiring healthcare providers to obtain state approval before building new hospitals, adding beds, purchasing major imaging equipment (MRI, CT), or opening ambulatory surgery centers. As of 2024, 35 states + DC have some form of CON regime; Texas, California, Ohio, and others have partially or fully repealed. T2: the SEEN rationale -- prevent 'duplicative' healthcare investment that would supposedly raise total costs; concentrate patients at a smaller number of facilities that will therefore have higher volume and better outcomes. T3: the UNSEEN Bastiat's method surfaces -- the CLINIC that never opens because the incumbent hospital objected to its CON application. In every CON state, existing hospitals routinely FILE OBJECTIONS to competitor applications, delaying approvals by years or defeating them entirely. Matthew Mitchell (Mercatus, multiple studies 2011-2020) documented that CON review is functionally a veto held by incumbents. Empirical findings: CON states have FEWER hospitals per capita, FEWER MRI machines per capita, and higher (not lower) per-service prices. T4: the specific IJ litigation -- the Institute for Justice's most-cited CON case is Baird v. Nebraska (2015 onward), Ursula Newell's medical transport service, and more recently Bogdanchik v. Kentucky Cabinet for Health and Family Services (2022) challenging Kentucky's home-health CON regime. IJ's argument: CON is an economic-protectionism regime that violates the 14th Amendment's protection of the right to earn a living, because it hands incumbent competitors the veto power over new entrants. name: The NYC taxi medallion: $1.3M to $100K after Uber
scope: The applied-Bastiat case where the unseen victim finally got heard through a market mechanism. T1: New York City has issued TAXI MEDALLIONS since the Haas Act 1937, capping the number of yellow-cab licenses in the city at ~11,700 through 2013. The medallion trades as a property right; the government's cap makes each one artificially scarce. T2: the SEEN pre-Uber -- medallion prices soared from $2,500 (1947) to $200,000 (1997) to a peak of ~$1.3 MILLION in 2013-14 (NYC Taxi and Limousine Commission auction data). Medallion owners were RICH; medallion drivers who leased from them worked long hours for modest income; NYC riders who could not find a cab in the rain simply went without service. T3: the UNSEEN Bastiat's method surfaces -- (1) the ~90,000 additional cabs the market wanted at the 2013 price, blocked by the cap; (2) the riders who could not get a cab and either waited, walked in bad weather, or drove drunk; (3) the outer-borough (Bronx, southeast Queens) residents who yellow cabs typically refused to serve. All three victims were invisible to the SEEN medallion market. T4: the DISRUPTION -- Uber launched in NYC 2011 (initially as a black-car service under a different regulatory category); by 2015 the app had bypassed the medallion cap entirely by categorizing every driver as a for-hire vehicle (FHV) rather than a taxi. Medallion prices COLLAPSED: from $1.3M (2013) to ~$700K (2016) to ~$100K (2019) -- an 92% loss of value for medallion owners who had borrowed against the medallion as collateral. The New York Times series 'Taxi Medallions Once a Safe Investment, Now Cause Financial Ruin' (Emma Fitzsimmons and Brian Rosenthal, May 2019) documented ~950 medallion-owner bankruptcies and 8 driver suicides. T5: Bastiat's method surfacing the WHOLE picture -- the medallion cap had for 76 years produced a VISIBLE class of wealthy medallion owners and an INVISIBLE class of denied riders and blocked would-be drivers. When technology (the smartphone) allowed the invisible class to organize supply outside the cap, the market immediately revealed what the cap had cost. The medallion owners' losses in 2013-19 are the CAPITALIZED value of the harm they had been extracting from riders and blocked drivers for decades; the transfer is painful for medallion owners, but it is a REVERSAL of a transfer that had run the OTHER way since 1937. This is the deep move: the previously-invisible costs of a policy become visible when the policy is bypassed.

name: Price-gouging laws: the generator that never leaves Georgia
scope: Applied-Bastiat for post-disaster price controls, framed through Mike Munger's Hurricane Frances gas-can story. T1: after every major US natural disaster, state attorneys general prosecute merchants who raise prices on essentials (gasoline, water, generators, plywood) as 'price gouging'. Most states have anti-price-gouging statutes; Florida's is triggered by any post-emergency-declaration sale at 'grossly exceeding' the pre-emergency price. T2: the SEEN advocates say -- prevent profiteering off desperate disaster victims; keep essentials affordable when families are most vulnerable. T3: the UNSEEN Bastiat's method surfaces -- the GENERATOR that never gets driven from Georgia to Miami because the entrepreneur cannot recoup his 800-mile round trip plus his own opportunity cost at a $50 price cap. Mike Munger (Duke political scientist / economist) has told the story for years: after Hurricane Fran September 1996, four entrepreneurs bought 100 bags of ice in Goldsboro NC at $1.75/bag, drove to Raleigh, and sold them at $12/bag to people whose refrigerators had been out for days. They were arrested for price-gouging. The people STANDING IN LINE to buy the ice at $12 were furious that the police shut down the sale, not at the sellers. T4: the KNOWLEDGE mechanism the prohibited price would have carried -- (1) the high price SIGNALS to distant suppliers that this location is a good place to send supplies; (2) it RATIONS scarce supply toward highest-value uses (the family with an insulin-dependent diabetic will pay for ice; the family who just wants cold drinks will wait); (3) it INCENTIVIZES conservation by existing holders. A $50 price cap on generators eliminates all three functions; the generator stays in Georgia, ice stays in Goldsboro, and the Miami family has neither. T5: John Stossel, Russ Roberts (EconTalk podcast), and Mike Munger have made this the canonical Bastiat-applied case for 25 years. Munger's essay 'They Clapped: Can Price-Gouging Laws Prohibit Scarcity?' Library of Economics and Liberty January 2007 is the reference text; his line: 'If you want less of something, tax it or make it illegal. Price-gouging laws make relief supplies illegal to sell to disaster victims.'

name: Corporate income tax: who actually pays
scope: Applied-Bastiat for tax-incidence reasoning. T1: the US corporate income tax (currently 21% federal since Tax Cuts and Jobs Act 2017; previously 35%) applies to C-corporation profits. Politicians campaigning on 'making corporations pay their fair share' present the tax as falling on corporate shareholders. T2: the SEEN -- Google, Apple, and Exxon write a check to the Treasury; the tax revenue line-item is 'corporate income tax'. T3: the UNSEEN economists ask -- INCIDENCE. When a corporation faces a tax on its profits, its response is to charge higher prices to CONSUMERS, pay lower wages to WORKERS, or accept lower returns to SHAREHOLDERS. Empirical labor-share research (Auten and Splinter 2019; CBO 2012 update to Distributional Effects tables; Suarez Serrato and Zidar AER 2016) estimates that between 50% and 100% of the corporate tax is ULTIMATELY borne by WORKERS through lower wages -- because capital is more mobile than labor, and mobile capital's after-tax return is set by world capital markets. T4: the intuition -- a corporation is a legal fiction; it cannot 'pay' a tax in any final sense. Every dollar of corporate tax comes from a real human's pocket: a consumer paying a higher price, a worker earning less, or a shareholder (who may be a pension fund holding retirement savings for teachers). Milton Friedman's line (Free to Choose 1980): 'Corporations do not pay taxes; only people pay taxes.' The politically SEEN benefit ('big corporations pay') is not the ECONOMIC UNSEEN reality (workers, consumers, and shareholders pay). T5: Bastiat's move -- the SEEN corporate-tax check is real; the UNSEEN wage-reduction, price-increase, and pension-return-reduction are dispersed across millions of workers, consumers, and shareholders. Because the incidence is dispersed and invisible, the political calculation always favors raising corporate taxes; the ECONOMIC reality is that the tax has been borne by ordinary workers all along. This is Bastiat's method applied to the most rhetorically effective tax populism.

name: Sarbanes-Oxley 2002: the small-cap IPOs that never happened

name: FDA drug approval: Peltzman and the patients who die waiting
scope: Applied-Bastiat for drug-approval regulation, the canonical Sam Peltzman case. T1: the 1962 Kefauver-Harris Amendments to the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, passed in the wake of the thalidomide-induced birth defects in Europe (thalidomide had NOT been approved in the US thanks to FDA reviewer Frances Kelsey's caution), required drug manufacturers to prove not just SAFETY but also EFFICACY to the FDA's satisfaction before marketing a new drug. T2: the SEEN effect -- fewer approved drugs turn out later to be ineffective or harmful; the FDA gains authority to demand efficacy trials before market entry. T3: the UNSEEN cost Sam Peltzman quantified in 1973 ('An Evaluation of Consumer Protection Legislation: The 1962 Drug Amendments' Journal of Political Economy 81 no 5, Sept-Oct 1973) -- new-drug introductions to the US market FELL by roughly HALF after 1962 relative to pre-1962 trends and relative to European drug markets. The 'drug lag' between US and European availability of new drugs grew to 2-5 years for many therapies. Peltzman's key insight: the UNSEEN cost is the patients whose disease had a treatment available in Europe but not yet in the US. T4: modern statement -- Alex Tabarrok (Marginal Revolution, GMU) has continued the argument through the 2010s and 2020s: the FDA's approval process asymmetrically weights Type I errors (approving a bad drug -- highly visible if a scandal ensues) against Type II errors (rejecting or delaying a good drug -- INVISIBLE because the deaths from the underlying disease look like ordinary deaths, not regulatory failures). During COVID (2020-21), the FDA's initial slow authorization of at-home rapid tests and Paxlovid restrictions became case studies of the same asymmetry. T5: Bastiat's method exact application -- SEEN: bad drugs blocked from market (visible headline). UNSEEN: patients dying of diseases whose treatment sits in the FDA queue. Peltzman's insight scales: any regulatory agency whose failures on one side are HEADLINES and whose failures on the other side are STATISTICS will systematically over-regulate the visible side and under-regulate the invisible side. This is Bastiat's method at the level of institutional design: the SEEN vs UNSEEN asymmetry becomes an institutional bias.

name: Dodd-Frank 2010: the community banks that consolidated
scope: Applied-Bastiat for post-2008 financial regulation. T1: the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act, signed July 21 2010 by President Obama, was the largest financial regulatory overhaul since the New Deal. It created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, imposed new capital and liquidity rules on banks, added the Volcker Rule limiting proprietary trading, and gave the FDIC new resolution authority. T2: the SEEN goal -- prevent a repeat of the 2008 financial crisis; protect consumers from predatory lending; end 'too big to fail'. T3: the UNSEEN Bastiat's method surfaces -- the COMPLIANCE COST fell disproportionately on SMALL COMMUNITY BANKS. Every Dodd-Frank rule required legal and compliance-officer staffing that a $500M-asset bank could not absorb the way a $500B-asset bank could. The number of US commercial banks fell from ~7,000 in 2010 to ~4,700 by 2023 (FDIC data -- CORROBORATE AT BUILD), with virtually no new bank charters granted 2010-16 (only 8 de novo bank charters approved by FDIC 2010-16 vs ~130/year in the 1990s and 2000s). T4: the concentrated-benefit / dispersed-cost pattern -- SEEN: consumer-protection rhetoric (concentrated moral advocacy). UNSEEN: the small business in a rural county whose community bank consolidated into a regional and no longer makes character-based small-business loans; the rural community with fewer bank branches; the Bootleggers-and-Baptists pattern (Yandle) where large money-center banks quietly benefited from the compliance-cost moat while the Baptists advocated the rules for consumer protection. name: Concealed carry fees: the victim who could not defend herself
scope: Applied-Bastiat for firearms-access regulation. T1: US states regulate concealed-carry-permit issuance through a spectrum ranging from 'constitutional carry' (no permit required, 27 states as of 2024) to 'may-issue' (permit granted at official discretion; NY, NJ, CA pre-Bruen 2022). Permit fees range from ~$25 (Kentucky) to ~$400+ with mandatory training (New York City historically); waiting periods run from days to months. T2: the SEEN advocates say -- fees and training requirements screen out unfit permit holders and generate revenue for administration. T3: the UNSEEN Bastiat's method surfaces -- the LOW-INCOME urban resident (often minority) who cannot afford the $400 fee and 20 hours of training and therefore does NOT get a permit and therefore cannot legally carry a firearm for self-defense. John Lott (More Guns, Less Crime, U. of Chicago Press 1998, 3rd ed 2010) documented that jurisdictions with lower fees and shall-issue standards had substantially higher permit uptake among lower-income and minority populations -- exactly the populations most likely to live in high-crime neighborhoods and most in need of self-defense capability. T4: the CONSTITUTIONAL argument the Supreme Court adopted in NYSRPA v. Bruen June 23 2022 (Justice Thomas) -- the Second Amendment protects a right to carry firearms outside the home; may-issue regimes that let officials deny permits absent 'proper cause' are unconstitutional. Post-Bruen, restrictive states have shifted to imposing high fees, extensive training requirements, and 'sensitive place' restrictions -- attempting to achieve the same restrictive result through cost rather than discretion. T5: Bastiat's move -- SEEN: revenue-generating fees, mandatory training, waiting periods (visible policy). UNSEEN: the woman being stalked by an ex-partner who cannot afford the $400+20-hours to legally carry, and who is disarmed against her attacker; the corner-store owner in Detroit who cannot afford the fee; the minority urban resident whose neighborhood the police cannot reliably protect. The victim who defends herself successfully appears in no statistic (Lott's DGU / defensive-gun-use estimates put such cases in the hundreds of thousands per year); the victim who was disarmed appears in the crime statistics indistinguishably from any other crime victim.

name: Airline deregulation 1978: the low-cost carriers the CAB blocked
scope: The applied-Bastiat / public-choice case where the unseen victim DID get heard and the regulation was repealed. T1: from 1938 to 1978, the US Civil Aeronautics Board (CAB) regulated interstate airline routes, fares, and market entry. To fly a new city pair, an airline had to apply for CAB permission; the CAB denied virtually all new-entrant applications 1938-78, allocating routes only among the existing 'trunk carriers' (Pan Am, American, TWA, United, etc). Fares were set by the CAB. T2: the SEEN case for the regulation -- protect legacy carriers from 'destructive' competition; maintain service to smaller cities through cross-subsidy; guarantee employment and unionized wages. T3: the UNSEEN Alfred Kahn (Cornell economist, appointed CAB chairman by Jimmy Carter 1977) documented -- (1) INTRASTATE fares in California (Pacific Southwest Airlines) and Texas (Southwest Airlines, flying only intrastate to escape CAB jurisdiction) were ~50% BELOW comparable interstate fares. This was the direct empirical proof that CAB was raising fares far above competitive levels. (2) LOW-COST business models the CAB had blocked for 40 years (point-to-point single-cabin flying) were being demonstrated in the two loophole markets. T4: the Airline Deregulation Act 1978 (signed October 24 by President Carter, largely drafted by Kahn's team) phased out CAB fare and route regulation over five years; the CAB was abolished January 1985. The predicted results all materialized: real airfares FELL ~40% (1978 to 2000, BLS data), passenger volume TRIPLED, low-cost carriers (Southwest expanded interstate, later JetBlue, Spirit, Frontier) emerged, and small-city service SHIFTED from subsidized trunk-carrier stops to hub-and-spoke connections through regional airlines. T5: the PUBLIC-CHOICE lesson -- the LOUDEST fight against deregulation came from the INCUMBENT trunk airlines and their PILOT UNIONS (ALPA), exactly the parties the regulation had protected for 40 years. This is Stigler's regulatory-capture pattern (the industry had captured the CAB) refuted in real time: once policymakers looked at the intrastate data, they could SEE the previously-unseen consumers paying above-competitive fares, and the political case collapsed. Airline deregulation is Bastiat's method vindicated as public policy: the UNSEEN victims were made visible, and the policy was rolled back.

name: The Cobra Effect: British Delhi and the bounty that backfired
scope: The perverse-incentive parable for the whole pillar. T1: during the British colonial administration of Delhi (the story is variously dated to the late 19th century; standard tellings cite the term as coming from German economist Horst Siebert's 2001 book Der Kobra-Effekt), the local government was concerned about the number of venomous cobras in the city. T2: the SEEN policy solution -- pay a BOUNTY per dead cobra brought to the government office. Kill more cobras = get paid; the population should fall. T3: the UNSEEN behavioral response -- entrepreneurial Delhi residents began BREEDING COBRAS for the bounty. Producing dead cobras in their own back yards was more profitable than hunting wild ones. The bounty had created a farming operation, not a hunting operation. T4: the SECOND-order response -- when the government eventually noticed the perverse incentive and CANCELED the bounty, the breeders were left with cobra stock they no longer had a market for. They RELEASED the snakes into the streets. Delhi's cobra population END the program HIGHER than it had been at the beginning. T5: the GENERALIZED lesson -- Siebert's Cobra Effect and Charles Goodhart's law ('when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure', 1975) name the same phenomenon: any policy that pays a bounty on an INDIRECT measure of the desired outcome creates incentives to game the measure rather than to produce the outcome. Applied cases: (a) Wells Fargo employees opening fake accounts to meet a cross-sell bounty (2016 scandal); (b) US public-school 'teaching to the test' when funding was tied to standardized test scores (NCLB 2001-15); (c) US hospital 30-day-readmission penalties leading hospitals to keep patients in the emergency department under observation rather than admit them (CMS penalties, ACA 2010); (d) academic publication metrics leading to salami-sliced papers and paper mills. Bastiat's method is the DEEP form of this move: any policy sets up incentives, and the UNSEEN response to those incentives is what will drive behavior.

name: Comparative advantage in reverse: what protectionism costs the poor
scope: Applied-Bastiat for the incidence of trade barriers across income levels. T1: modern US trade policy applies HIGHER tariff rates to LOW-END consumer goods (imported shoes, clothing, cheap electronics) than to LUXURY goods. Average US tariff on cheap sneakers (~15-20%) vs on high-end leather dress shoes (~5-8%); tariffs on children's clothes (~15%) vs on cashmere sweaters (~5%). This is not accidental -- domestic producers of low-end goods lobbied hardest for protection, and their trade-lobby lawyers wrote the tariff schedule. T2: the SEEN -- domestic footwear and apparel firms retain some US employment; the tariffs appear in Chapter 61-64 of the Harmonized Tariff Schedule as small percentages. T3: the UNSEEN Ed Gresser (Progressive Policy Institute, later USTR) documented in 'Toughest on the Poor: America's Flawed Tariff System' (PPI 2002; later work in 2019 for PPI): the LOW-INCOME US household spends a much higher share of income on the tariffed goods (cheap shoes, cheap clothes, cheap kitchenware) than the high-income household spends on cashmere. Effective tariff burden on the bottom household-income quintile is roughly 3-4x the burden on the top quintile as a share of income. T4: the applied Bastiat move -- SEEN: revenue and preserved-job talking points. UNSEEN: the working-mother in a Dollar General household paying an effective 15% surcharge on her family's shoes and clothes because the tariff schedule was written by the same industry lobbyists who lobbied for the tariffs. The tariff functions as a HIGHLY REGRESSIVE consumption tax -- more regressive than any sales tax, because it targets specifically the goods the poor buy most. T5: the DEEPEST Bastiat move here -- protectionism's most effective political argument is 'protect American jobs', invoking working-class solidarity. The Bastiat method reveals that the same protectionism is a REGRESSIVE TAX on working-class households, more punishing to the bottom quintile than to the top. Sowell in Basic Economics: 'The people who claim to be defending American workers with tariffs are taxing the American workers most.' Choice for the pupil: recognize the reasoning move, and judge for oneself.
